title: NEOSTI - a neuromorphic electronic-opto spatial-temporal hybrid image sensor

paper_content.abstract: Image sensors in machine vision systems face significant challenges related to energy efficiency and processing capability when storing, transferring, and processing massive amounts of data. In humans, over 80% of brain-processed information is obtained through the eyes, which are capable of detecting and synchronously processing information with extremely low overall power consumption. Inspired by the biomimetics, we propose a Neuromorphic Electronic-Opto Spatial Temporal Imager (NEOSTI), one of the smallest electronic-opto fully integrated, eye-sized vision systems enabling acquisition and operation in typical indoor/outdoor non-coherent environments, under both natural and artificial lighting conditions without any extra requirement of the light source. NEOSTI combines processing-pre-sensor in optical domain, processing-in-sensor with nonlinear acquisition capability while optical to electronic converting, and processing-near-sensor in electronic domain, enabling parallel data computing capabilities while sensing. NEOSTI also integrates a low complexity Binary Neural Network to process image semantic information. It attains competitive performance in several visual processing tasks.
paper_content.introduction:
The human visual system is highly efficient in collecting and processing of the visible information. As a bionic device, the image sensor establishes a bridge between the real world in optical domain and artificial intelligence in electronic domain, but current image sensor technology falls short in meeting the requirement of real-time, low-power processing capability at the edge, which is critical for embodied intelligence such as intelligent robots, fully autonomous driving, and drones that require effective interaction with dynamic environments. Different processing technologies in either electronic domain or optical domain have been proposed in literature to break the bottleneck, but there is always a trade-off between processing performance and power/volume consumption.

Traditional artificial vision system relies on image sensors coupled with cloud processing or Artificial Intelligence (AI) processors, featuring higher image resolution, higher frame rate, and higher accuracy across various image processing tasks than human visual system, but paying for a several orders higher power consumption than the human visual system. In addition, the sub second wireless communication latency [1] between the sensor end and the computational cloud cannot meet the milliseconds to sub-milliseconds response time requirement risen from the embodied intelligence scenario.

In order to improve efficiency of the traditional artificial vision system, Processing-in-Sensor (PIS) [2–9] and Processing-Near-Sensor (PNS) [10–12] technologies have been introduced into the raw intensity acquisition process. PIS/PNS technology mitigates the delay and power consumption associated with redundant data transmission workload by integrating the sensing and computing components, enhances data processing efficiency as well as reduces the volume of data transmitted to the host through parallel processing at column or pixel levels. This approach aligns more closely with the operational principles of the visual systems observed in humans and various creatures. Nevertheless, the interdependence of the sensing and computing ends, influenced by the manufacturing process, implies that the performance of one end can impact the other, and the computing capabilities achievable on the sensing end are inherently limited.

In addition to PIS/PNS in electronic domain, optical domain calculation also provides a promising solution to increase computing speed without greatly increase the power consumption, as well as to overcome the bandwidth bottlenecks of PIS/PNS. In particular, the optical solution enables compression in the spatial domain of the image, resulting in a reduction of the amount of data to be processed on the sensor side. The development of the neural networks using optical methods, commonly referred to as optical neural networks (ONNs), has gained considerable traction as a prominent research area. Different ONNs have been proposed in literature [13–15], realizing parallel information processing by integrating optical architecture based on free space, aiming to accelerate deep learning computation. However, ONNs faces constraints related to power consumption, data rate, and on-chip processing capabilities. Additionally, many ONNs have restriction on light source, such as specific coherent light source, which cannot work in natural light condition.

In this article, we propose an all-in-one neuromorphic electronic-opto spatial-temporal image sensor (NEOSTI) design, which integrates various technologies to enhance data processing efficiency as well as to reduce sensor volume size. The NEOSTI integrated processing-pre-sensor(PPS) in optical domain, PIS with nonlinear acquisition capability and parallel data computing capabilities while sensing, and PNS with an on-chip binary neural network (BNN) for image semantic information processing. The NEOSTI attains competitive performance in five static and dynamic visual processing tasks. The experimental results reveal an accuracy of 96.4% in MNIST (10-category), 94.9% in UnityEyes (4-category), 91.7% in QuickDraw (10-category), 91.3% in Fashion MNIST (10-category), and 90.6% in Weizmann (video, 10-category), which demonstrate significant advancements in accuracy across multiple categories. These findings demonstrate a compact and efficient vision system with potential applications across a range of scenarios. Table 1 summarizes and compares the NEOSTI with representative frontier work in the fields discussed above. The NEOSTI is one of the smallest electronic-opto fully integrated vision systems that can operate in typical indoor and outdoor environments, under both natural and artificial lighting conditions, without any extra requirement of the light source, such as laser or coherent light source.
paper_content.results:
Architecture of NEOSTI

The human visual system (Fig.1a) enables efficient information compression while acquisition. There are over 130 million photoreceptor cells located in retina converting illumination intensity into neural spike signal. However, since a significant amount of pre-processing occurs within the retina itself [27], only about 1.2 million fibers (axons) are required in the optic nerve, resulting in an equivalent compression ratio of over 100. In addition, the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN) in the visual pathway plays a role in attenuating temporal correlations within the image, which further reduces the total amount of neural signals to be processed in the visual cortex. Secondly, the retina consumes only about 3 mW for both intensity acquisition and fundamental feature extraction [28], realizing a 23.08 pW/pixel energy efficiency. While state-of-the-art consumer image sensors only achieve an efficiency around 30 nW/pixel [29] for only intensity acquisition. In addition, the human visual system enables an intra-scene dynamic range (DR) of over 120 dB [28] and an inter-scene DR over 180 dB. While consumer image sensors typically achieve a DR of only 60-70 dB, the most advanced of which reaches around 140 dB [30].

Inspired by biomimetics, NEOSTI (Fig.1b) incorporates similar functionalities, including computations throughout the entire process, closely mimicking the capabilities of biological systems. The workflow of NEOSTI (Fig.1c) starts from a sliding convolution in the optical domain. A mask is deployed in front of the photodetector array in the electrical domain, filtering the input images and extracting the spatial features, which effectively reduces the amount of data received on the sensor plane. Subsequently, visual information is further processed using nonlinear optoelectronic conversion together with a calculation-supported readout link of the pixel circuit. At last, a low-complexity on-chip BNN is implemented as the visual cortex, providing high-level information processing capabilities, and finally obtaining the end-to-end classification result.

NEOSTI can be equivalent to an algorithm model (Fig.1d), which combines the optical domain and the electrical domain to construct a 3-layer sliding convolutional neural network. Initially, the 3-layer neural network model is trained to obtain the parameters for each part of the network. Subsequently, the parameters of the first layer’s 5 × 5 convolution kernel are extracted, binarized and solidified into physical patterns. The remaining of the network is reprogramed into a reconfigurable chip. The convolution mask and chip are co-packaged forming a lensless vision chip, which is capable of being fabricated using a mature process, making it well-suited for large-scale production.

Pre-sensor Processing in Optical Domain

The human eye (Fig.2a) perceives a world full of vibrant colors, while each animal has its distinct method of processing visual information. For instance, the compound eyes (Fig.2b) of flies are highly specialized, capable of capturing images at remarkable speeds. Their visual nervous system is adapted to rapidly process moving objects, enabling them to detect and react to their environment with high efficiency. Pre-processing occurs directly within the fly’s eyes for promptly responding to movement in their surroundings. Similarly, in frogs, specialized neurons in the retina are responsible for detecting edges or sudden motions within a scene. These neurons aid frogs in their survival strategies for hunting prey or evading predators. By filtering and integrating varying levels of light intensity and boundary information, a sophisticated feature detection is performed to ensure rapid and precise visual processing.

NEOSTI (Fig.2c) serves as the ”eyes” for machines, such as robots, facilitating intelligent processing across a variety of scenarios. It combines the capability of human eyes for the acquisition of the imaging of a scene, and compound eyes for feature extraction. The incident scene passes through four convolution kernels on the mask (Fig.2d), resulting in four feature maps on the sensor. The sliding convolution calculation is completed through the projection relationship of the geometric optics. Each pixel value on the feature map is obtained in parallel with near-zero latency. The schematic diagram of the equivalent optical calculation of the mask can be represented in a 5 × 5 binary matrix (Fig.2e). Assume that the input light source consists of a series of point light sources, by adjusting the distance from the mask to the imaging plane, each pixel on the imaging plane can receive the convolutional result between the point light source within a specific region and the convolution kernel parameters on the mask. As a result, the sensor plane receives four parallel convolution feature maps (Fig.2f). The feature size of the mask is limited by both diffraction and optical blur. (Fig.2g). Leveraging the propagation characteristics of geometric optics, this process can be effectively represented as a window sliding convolution, which is performed in parallel. The PPS operates at the position of the lens or glasses within the human visual system, augmenting the system’s capabilities and enabling direct processing of optical domain data, which is an attribute absence in the human visual system. By processing information in the optical domain, data arriving at the PIS module can be compressed with near-zero latency and zero power consumption, thereby reducing power consumption in both photoelectric conversion and data processing stages.

Neuromorphic Nonlinear Photoelectric Response

The retina, situated at the back of the eye, is a layered structure responsible for capturing light and initiating the process of vision (Fig.3a). The cones and rods in the lowest layer serve as photoreceptors, generating bio-signals associated with light intensity. The signal is then conveyed and transmitted through cells in the middle region of the retina. Ultimately, the generated nerve impulses are traveling along the optic nerve tract. The impulses are subsequently relayed to the visual cortex in the brain.

In a Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor, a reverse-biased photodiode structure is employed as the photoreceptors for photoelectric conversion (Fig.3d). The photodiode generates a photocurrent that is positively correlated with light intensity. A pre-reset capacitor is discharged by the photocurrent, causing the voltage VPD to decrease at a rate contingent upon the light intensity, realizing a conversion from optical intensity to electrical signals. The signals are subsequently amplified and read out by the associated circuit. Typically, a voltage-readout pixel structure is utilized. It is also known as the accumulation-mode pixel structure (Fig.3b), in which the voltage drop, ∆VPD, over a certain exposure time is measured and read out via an analog-to-digital convertor (ADC) to obtain the corresponding digital code value (Fig.3c), resulting in a linear relationship for the light-to-voltage conversion (gray line in Fig.3i).

Conversely, the human visual system employs a nonlinear relationship between the light intensity and perception is employed due to the nonlinearity of photoreceptor response (Fig.3j). This nonlinear characteristic effectively expands the visual capacity to a wider range of light levels, particularly in extremely bright or dim environments.

Inspired by the human vision system, NEOSTI utilizes a pulse width modulated (PWM) based 3-layered readout pixel structure [31–33] (Fig.3e), realizing a retina-mimicking nonlinear photoresponse and pulse-based representation of light intensity. The fundamental principle of the pulse modulation method starts with setting a voltage threshold at the configuration stage. A pulse flip was triggered when the voltage on the photodiode reaches the preset threshold VINV during the exposure process (Fig.3f). This approach enables a nonlinear light-to-time conversion without the requirement of ADC, and allows operation at lower voltages. The pulse output format also facilitates low-power computation design at the circuit level processing, which will be discussed in the following section. To further align the nonlinear response of PWM pixel with the human eye, a dynamic scanning bias voltage, VG, is applied at point G (Fig.3g), making the threshold of the flipping voltage VINV to gradually increase over time. Compared to a fixed flipping voltage threshold, dynamic VINV stretches the response curve in low-light intensity ranges, extending the dynamic range of pixel under dark light condition (Fig.3h-i). Experimental results indicate that the PWM pixels of NEOSTI exhibit a nonlinear photoresponse function similar to that of visual cells to encode light intensity information (Fig.3k). Moreover, the simulated responses demonstrate that by adjusting the bias voltage VG, the pixel has the potential to mimic the adaptive function of the human eye, shifting the curve as a whole to accommodate varying lighting conditions (Fig.3l).

In-Sensor and Near-Sensor Processing

Behind the photosensitive area, an array of processing elements (PEs) is employed to receive the pulse signal, enabling parallel visual information in-sensor processing. The processing element is simultaneously connected to two adjacent PWM pixels (Fig.4a), performing direct summation or subtraction calculation on the two pulse signals from two neighboring pixels based on programmable parameters during the exposure process. The working times of the two counters within the PE are non-overlapping (Fig.4b), which reduces the counters’ working duration by 33% compared to conventional readout methods, lowering circuit dynamic power consumption. The summation calculation is performed using a left-shift module for efficient ”×2” operation, and a digital adder to sum the digital codes, while the subtraction calculation relies solely on counter DIFF, allowing counter SUM to be disabled to achieve greater performance advantages. The overall in-sensor processing forms part of a 2 × 2 binary convolution with a stride of 1, which effectively removes spatial-temporal redundancy and extract fundamental features from the input data.

Additionally, a BNN is implemented on-chip, providing advanced near-sensor information processing capabilities, and enhancing the ability to generalize across various tasks. Due to the concurrent exposure of each row of pixels and the simultaneous generation of intra-row calculation results by parallel PEs, the implementation of a pipeline architecture becomes imperative to efficiently execute convolution operations. A 4-stage pipeline dedicated to a convolution block (Fig.4c) is utilized in NEOSTI. The block encompasses a 2 × 2 convolution layer, a ReLU nonlinear activation function, and a 2 × 2 maximum pooling layer. This pipelined architecture is compactly parallelized, fully utilizing the row-by-row exposure time of the pixels to complete the pipeline operations without any additional time overhead, maximizing the utilization of on-chip hardware resources with high computational efficiency. There are in total two layers of convolution and pooling operations performed through the in-sensor and the near-sensor processing, yielding the fully-processed feature maps. By leveraging on-chip storage capabilities, the difference between frames can be directly calculated, which is a commonly-used operation for inter-frame processing. Combined with subsquent pipelined BNN structure, NEOSTI is endowed with enhanced ability for processing spatial-temporal hybrid information.

Evaluation of NEOSTI system

The performance of NEOSTI has been validated across multiple tasks, including MNIST[34], Fashion MNIST[35], Quick Draw[36] and UnityEyes[37], with an accuracy of 96.4%, 91.3%, 91.7%, and 94.9%, respectively (Fig.5a). In experiments, the opticalmaskkeptthesameconvolutionpattern,whiletheparametersofelectricallayerswere reconfigured for different tasks. The experimental results not only show the recognition performance of NEOSTI on various tasks, but also demonstrate that the programmableelectricalconvolutionlayersprovideNEOSTIwithgoodgeneralization ability between different tasks.

In order to further verify the respective functions of each part of NEOSTI, differentsetups,includingexperimentsusingonlyPPSoronlyPIS,wereverifiedseparately (Fig.5b). The NEOSTI shows an average accuracy improvement of 11.725% and 14.075%comparedwithonlyPISoronlyPPS.ComparedwithLeNet-5,asmallneural network in the digital domain, NEOSTI shows similar performance. In addition, we also verified the noise robustness of NEOSTNI (Fig.5c) using the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) calculated as
PSNR=10·log(MAXI)2/MSE=20·log(MAXI/√MSE) (1)
where MAXI represents the maximum pixel value, and MSE represents the noise level. When the light intensity becomes lower, the PSNR deteriorates. Experimental results show that when the PSNR decreases, NEOSTI does not significantly deteriorate in the accuracy of different characters. This feature is advantageous due to the fact that the optical domain processing enables the filtration of a portion of the noise. Furthermore, the neural network’s robust anti-interference capability enables better performance, particularly in low-light photo scenarios.

In addition to static image classification task, NEOSTI was also tested on the video analysis task, which requires not only the capability of spatial information acquistion, but also the capability of temporal information analysis between frames. NEOSTI is evaluated on an open dataset, Weizmann [38]. The Weizmann dataset (Fig.5d) includes multiple video sequences of ten different actions, including run, jump, bend, etc. In each video sequence, only one person performs the action. NEOSTI can convert sequence information into several feature maps (Fig.5g), with an accuracy of 90.6% (Fig.5e). The BNN-based feature extraction model serves as a general, real-time, and efficient data compressor that effectively reduces the input data volume by 81.3%, significantly reducing the computational and storage overhead of feature sequences while preserving intra-frame spatial features. In different-setup experiments, the only PPS setup shows a 58% accuracy on the same dataset (Fig.5f). This is mainly due to the fact that the processing of the optical domain is spatially without storage. The programmable on-chip PIS and PNS circuits can make up for this. Similarly to the test on static image classification task, when noise increases, NEOSTI exhibits good robustness (Fig.5h). The spatial domain filtering of the PPS module still plays a key role in processing noise.

Design of optical domain convolution mask

Anopticalmaskwasappliedinfrontofthepixelarrayinsteadofalens(Supplementary Fig. 1a) to realize the calculation of one-layer convolution.
As a result, there are four 5 × 5 binary convolution kernel patterns representing the pre-trained convolution kernel parameters (0 or 1) of the first layer of the BNN (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The feature size of the kernel pattern, ∆, was set to 40 µm (Supplementary Fig. 1c) to satisfy ∆≥ (2.44λd)/K to avoid the diffraction effect withalightsourcewavelength,λ,of405nm.Thepitchsize(d)wascalculatedtobe 1.28 mm (Supplementary Fig. 1a) to achieve a coverage of one-quarter sensor array (about 1.28 mm × 1.28 mm) by each kernel pattern, as well as to generate 4 non-overlap feature maps for the following layer. According to the theory of geometrical optics, the sensor plane captures the light signal S0,S1,...,Sm−1 as an outcome of sliding multiplication and accumulation between the light source, L0,L1,...,Ln−1, and the mask. This is a parallel computing process with no power consumption and almost zero latency.

The aperture ratio of the optical mask is approximately 50%. Additionally, the mask template is fabricated using a process where a coating is applied to a glass substrate. Due to losses caused by refraction and other factors in the glass substrate, when the pixel is set to be transparent, the transmission rate is approximately 90%. Therefore, the overall transmission rate is 45%. The light intensity attenuation caused by modulation, refraction, and other factors is approximately 3.47 dB.

Retina-inspired photoreceptors and pulse modulation

ThePWMpixelstructuregeneratesdifferentwidthspulsesignalstorepresentdifferent light intensities. This architectural configuration offers two benefits: 1) its dynamic rangeremainsunrestrictedbypowersupplyvoltage(VDD)constraints,facilitatingits operationevenatexceptionallylowerpowersupplylevers,thusrenderingitamenable forenergy-efficientcomputationaltasks;2)theresultantoutputsignalisdirectlydigital signal, obviating the conventional necessity for an ADC, and seamlessly integrating into computational processes. In this work, all the transistors are operated in the sub-threshold region under a VDD of 0.35 V. Its working process is realized by a current comparator composed of two transistors, MP and MN (Supplementary Fig. 2a). In the exposure phase, VPD is discharged by the bias current source, resulting in an exponential increase of the drain current of MP. Simultaneously, the decrease of VPD leads to a reduction in the drain current of MN. IP and IN are denoted as:
IP=IP0×exp((VDD-VG-VTH,P)/(npVT)) (3)
IN=IN0×exp((VPD-VTH,N)/(nnVT)) (4)
With exposure, IP gradually becomes larger than IN, causing the voltage at node VOUT is pulled up. At this moment, IP is approximately equal to IN, (3) and (4) yield:
VPD,INV=nn/(np+nn)*(VDD-VG,INV-VTH,P)+nn/(np+nn)*VT*ln(IP0/IN0)+VTH,N (5)
ThepulsewidthTINV,correspondingtothetimeelapsedfromthestartofexposure to the moment when the voltage VPD is flipped, is proportional to the incident light intensity (Supplementary Fig. 2b), which can be calculated as:
TINV=CPD*(VPD,RST-VPD,INV)/(Iph-IP0*exp((VDD-VG,INV-VTH,P)/(npVT)))
For dynamic scanning bias voltage applied in our work, VG is represented by TINV as:
VG,INV=VG0-k·TINV (7)
where k is the slope of the scanning bias voltage change with respect to time (Fig.3.g).

To balance the trade-off between power consumption and noise performance in different pixel working mode, two distinct reset strategies are implemented in the acquisition mode and the calculation mode, respectively. This is achieved by adding a cascode transistor MR to the typical PWM pixel structure (as shown in Supplementary Fig.2a), which controls the on/off state of the current path during the reset phase.

In the acquisition mode, the low-noise reset approach is applied to eliminate the threshold voltage mismatch noise, which is described as follows. The switch SW2 is closed during the reset phase, connecting the drain and gate of the NMOS transistor MN. When the charge is fully reset on the PD, there will be no current passing through this branch. Then the transistor MR is turned on, establishing a current path VDD-MP-MR-MN-VSS, which ensures the initial IP = IN. The reset voltage of the photodiode can be derived from (3) and (4) as:
VPD,RST=nn/(np+nn)*(VDD-VG,RST-VTH,P)+nn/(np+nn)*VT*ln(IP0/IN0)+VTH,N (8)
At the time TINV, The difference of the two voltages VPD,RST and VPD,INV is:
∆VPD=VPD,RST-VPD,INV=nn/(np+nn)*(VG,INV-VG,RST) (9)
The∆VPD issolelydependentonthedisparitiesbetweennp,nn andVG,effectively mitigatingvariationsinducedbythefabricationprocessandsuppressingcolumnFPN.

In the calculation mode, the transistor MR is turned off to interrupt the flow of DC current from MP to ground through MN to achieve a low-power reset, which reduces the average current in the reset phase to 0.17% of that in the on state, leading to a 31% reduction in the average power consumption per row time. Although the threshold mismatch noise is not eliminated, experiments conducted in the calculation mode show that a 1% pixel value deviation leads to only about a 0.2% decrease in classification accuracy. In addition, the PE eliminates most of the errors when calculating sum/differential of the adjacent pixels. As a result, the noise caused by non-ideal factors has little impact in the calculation mode.

The pipeline structure of neural network

Duetotheconcurrentexposureofeachrowofpixelsandthesimultaneousgeneration of intra-row calculation results by 64 PEs, the implementation of a pipeline architecture becomes imperative to efficiently execute convolution operations. Supplementary Fig.4a illustrates the design and workflow of a 4-stage pipeline dedicated to a convolution block. This block encompasses a 2 × 2 convolution layer, a ReLU function, and a 2 × 2 maximum pooling layer. The hardware structure of the convolution block is illustrated in Supplementary Fig.4b, which is implemented directly after the PEs of each column. The specific process of the 4-stage pipeline is described as follows:
Cycle 1: 64 PEs compute and generate the 2 × 1 outputs, PEOUT0(m) and PEOUT1(m), for the mth row of pixels, where, RES0 and RES1 are the convolution results of the two adjacent pixel values with the first and second rows of the convolution kernel K = [k0,k1;k2,k3], respectively.
For the nth column of pixels, RES0 and RES1 are calculated as
RES0(m,n)=k0·IN(n)+k1·IN(n+1)
RES1(m,n)=k2·IN(n)+k3·IN(n+1)
The output result of PEOUT0(m) will be cached to Cycle 2.
Cycle2:ThecachedresultPEOUT0(m)issummedwithPEOUT1(m+1)togenerate the 2 × 2 convolution results for the mth and (m+1)th row. The convolution results then pass through the ReLU activation function module, whose hardware structure is a 2-to-1 multiplexer controlled by the sign bit of the input (Supplementary Fig.4c) : if the sign bit is 0 (indicating a positive value), the original data is passed through; if the sign bit is 1 (indicating a negative value), a value of zero is output. The outputs of convolution and ReLU activation(denoted as CM(m)) are stored to Cycle 3.
CM(m)=ReLU(PEOUT0(m)+PEOUT1(m+1)) (12)
Cycle 3: The 2 × 1 maximum pooling,which is implemented in hardware using a comparator and a 2-to-1 multiplexer (Supplementary Fig.4d), is performed within the row direction. And the output result MP(m) is cached to Cycle 4.
MP(m,n/2)=Max(CM(m,n)+CM(m,n+1)) (13)
Cycle 4: Another 2 × 1 maximum pooling module is applied to the previously cached result MP(m) and the newly generated result MP(m+1) from the last stage, producing the final 2×2 maximum pooling result.
OUT(m/2,n/2)=Max(MP(m,n/2),MP(m+1,n/2)) (14)
With the pipelined calculating hardware structure, the processing results of one standard BNN layer can be completed synchronously with the pixel exposure, generating the feature map in a row-by-row scheme as well.
During the processing, the quantization bit-width varies with each operation. The specific bit-widths following each operation are listed in Supplementary Fig.8. The raw image is quantized as 10-bit unsigned integers. After processing through the two-layer electrical network, the resulting feature map is quantized as 15-bit signed integers.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In “NEOSTI: A Neuromorphic Electronic-Opto Spatial-Temporal Hybrid Image Sensor”, Tianyi Liu and co-authors present a
study on an all-in-one, fully integrated vision system that combines optical pre-processing, in-sensor and near-sensor
processing, and on-chip binary neural network (BNN) computation. The system is capable of operating under both natural
and artificial lighting conditions without the need for coherent light sources. This paper is innovative and is of interest to
potential readers working in the field of machine vision and edge computing. There are some comments on this work listed
as follows:
Q1: The optical mask in front of the chip systems is not new. It is better for the author to discuss the feasibility of
implementing reconfigurable or programmable optical masks, or alternative approaches to enhance flexibility for different
tasks or datasets.
Q2: The manuscript introduces the use of pulse width modulated (PWM) to encode light intensity, which is then processed
by on-chip units for arithmetic operations and subsequent processing by a binary neural network (BNN) in a pipelined
fashion without the requirement of ADC. The computing process is all realized in digital domain. While this is an interesting
approach, since current in-memory computing strategies usually conduct the matrix multiplication operation in analog
domain by converting the signal into an output voltage intensity, which is applicable to ANN with multi-valued weight
parameters. The authors could explained more about whether the benefits of pulse width coding are unique to BNNs or
applicable to a broader class of models.
Q3: The system relies on a combination of in-sensor processing (PIS) and near-sensor binary neural network (PNS) to
handle dynamic scenes. The speed advantage of BNNs in conducting dynamic tasks is not sufficiently discussed or
demonstrated. A more detailed analysis of these points would significantly strengthen the paper and improve its clarity, such
as the advantages of NEOSTI compares to established dynamic processing approaches such as in-sensor or in-memory
recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)1 or dynamic vision sensors (DVS)2. Also, is the time resolution of this NEOSTI will be
limited by the row-by-row exposure mode?.
Q3: While the manuscript describes the overall system architecture and the role of the on-chip BNN, it lacks a detailed
account of the BNN hardware implementation. For completeness and to facilitate reproducibility, I recommend that the
authors provide more information regarding the hardware structure of the BNN module.
I recommend that the manuscript be considered for publication after the authors have adequately addressed the above
comments through further discussion and revisions.
1. Chen, J. et al. Optoelectronic graded neurons for bioinspired in-sensor motion perception. Nature Nanotechnology 18,
882-888 (2023).
2. Zhou, Y. et al. Computational event-driven vision sensors for in-sensor spiking neural networks. Nature Electronics 6,
870-878 (2023).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors propose a new Neuromorphic Electronic–Opto Spatial–Temporal Imager to enhance data processing efficiency
and reduce the overall sensor volume.
Overall, I find that more information about the image sensor array performance and features is needed. Below, I provide
some comments to guide the authors in improving the article’s content:
1. Include a table of specific image sensor features.
The following key parameters appear to be missing and should be provided:
• Fill factor
• Sensor dynamic range (the authors claim both indoor and outdoor operation)
• Fixed-pattern noise
• Pixel power consumption
• Spatial contrast sensitivity (when computed from processed pixel outputs)
• Sensor latency versus illumination
• Any other relevant specifications
2. Clarifications on pixel and image sensor operation/implementation:
• What is the range of selectable integration times for system operation?
• At the pixel level, what is the purpose of the cascode transistor, and what is its bias value?
• Discuss how dark current limits the sensor’s dynamic range.
• The design requires a time-to-digital converter (TDC) to assign intensity levels based on pixel time response. How many
bits are used to implement the TDC? What is the range of pixel response times it can handle? How does TDC resolution
affect pixel dynamic range?
• Provide the system clock frequency.
• One of the claimed advantages of the proposed architecture is low power consumption. Please elaborate on the trade-off
between power consumption and frame rate.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The approach presented in this paper is certainly interesting from a scientific perspective. Splitting operations and layers of a
CNN-type network for image data processing (image recognition/classification tasks) between different physical elements
like static optical masks, focal-plane/pixel-level analog signal processing and binary neural network layers operated in the
digital domain, is an interesting and novel concept worth to be published. The presentation of innovation is sufficiently well
done, the idea, concept and methodology are well described and illustrated. Evaluation results are presented. However,
several points need to be addressed, in particular the discussion section is very weak and misses out on several key
questions.
In my view, at least these points below need to be addressed before possible publication of this material:
(1) Some claims are bold or imprecise:
"the smallest all-in-one eye size fully integrated vision system", The presented vision system, with chip dimensions of 5mm x
5mm is certainly not "the smallest" ever proposed. Just as one of many examples, Synsens's Speck vision System-on-Chip
combines a 128x128 (event-based) pixel array with a 9-layer spiking CNN processor on 30mm2 silicon.
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06793)
"Near-human performance in five static and dynamic visual processing tasks" — "near human" is a very bold statement,
particularly given the toy-problem like nature of the experiments/data sets used for validation of the NEOSTI approach, see
below (4).
"current image sensor technology falls short in meeting the requirement of embodied intelligence", a broad statement without
any clear meaning. Later, "embodied intelligence" is vaguely defined as possibly involving e.g. "intelligent robots, fully
autonomous driving, drones..."
"NEOSTI utilizes a pulse width modulated (PWM) based non-linear readout pixel structure, realizing a retina-like 3-layered
processing structure to generate pulse signals analogous to neural spikes" — NEOSTI is far from being "retina-like" or from
generating anything resembling "neural spikes". This is per se not a problem but does not need to be claimed this way.
(2) More issues not related to technical content that need attention:
Several language-related flaws: E.g. "NEOSTI is ... system that can operable ...", "lenless" — proof reading required
Factually imprecise statements: "consumer image sensor can only achieve a DR around 140dB" — no, consumer imagers
typically reach 60-70dB, only specialized automotive multi-exposure image sensors go up to DR levels around/beyond
140dB"
Citations and benchmarking: NEOSTI claims to be "neuromorphic" but does not compare itself to any other neuromorphic
vision solutions (e.g. event sensor based) that can solve similar problems; e.g. Synsense's Speck, combining event pixel
array and SNN processor on a single chip (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06793) nor with SoA industry Vision System-on-chip
solutions like Sony's IMX500, targeting similar use cases/applications (https://www.aitrios.sony-semicon.com/edge-ai-
devices/imx500).
Pulse modulation (including PWM) is a well known approach in vision sensing — prior work should be cited (e.g.
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5701724).
(3) Missing discussion on Static mask limitations:
Looking at the early feature extraction capabilities of NEOSTI, the static optical mask functions as the first convolutional
layer of a 3-layer convolutional neural network. The features it extracts are likely some fundamentally low-level spatial
features, determined by the patterns etched onto the mask itself. The mask performs a 5x5 sliding convolution on the
incoming light. I assume that this process is analogous to the initial feature extraction step in a typical CNN, which often
identifies basic elements like edges, corners, and textures. In the present case, the weights, implemented as the patterns on
the mask, are binary (transparent or opaque) and are derived from the pre-trained weights of a Binary Neural Network
(BNN). This means the mask is optimized for the types of features relevant to its original training data. For a different use
case requiring the detection of fundamentally different low-level features, a new mask would need to be fabricated. So, while
this optical pre-processing is highly efficient in terms of power and speed, a static, fabricated mask does present limitations
regarding flexibility and the range of addressable use cases.
In my view, a deeper discussion on this subject is missing and should include:
Lack of Adaptability: The mask itself cannot adapt to changing conditions or tasks at run-time. The system's adaptability
relies on the programmable on-chip electronic circuits (PIS and PNS) that process the feature maps created by the static
mask.
Potential for Sub-Optimal Performance on Unseen Tasks: The fixed front-end filtering might be sub-optimal for tasks that
were not considered during the initial training and mask design. The success of the system on a new task depends on
whether the features extracted by the fixed mask are still relevant and sufficiently informative for the subsequent electronic
layers to work with.
The paper suggests some kind of modular approach where optical components could be interchanged via a standardized
interface, allowing for task versatility. This implies that for different applications, one could swap out the mask for another
one with more suitable pre-trained patterns. How could such an approach be implemented in a real-world / commercial
scenario? I believe some in-depth discussion on these points would significantly increase the quality and impact of the
paper.
(4) Insufficient discussion on Adaptability and Scalability:
In my understanding, the presented implementation as described seems to have a limited real-world applicability. The
concept (in the form of a fabricated prototype) is validated only on "toy problems", using very low-resolution input data with
only simple high-contrast grey scale or BW features. (MNIST, UnityEyes, QuickDraw, Fashion MNIST, Weizmann), and the
NEOSTI approach, in its current form, would face considerable challenges when applied to more complex, higher-resolution,
and full grayscale natural scenes. The limitations I think is the binary optical mask.
Higher-Resolution Features: Scaling to a higher resolution would present a physical challenge due to light diffraction. The
minimum feature size that can be created on the optical mask is governed by the wavelength of light and the distance
between the mask and the sensor. Currently, the feature size is set to 40µm. To increase the image resolution, the pixels on
the sensor would need to be made smaller and more numerous. Consequently, the features on the mask would also need to
shrink to match this new, finer pixel grid. However, as the feature size shrinks, the diffraction of light becomes a more
significant issue, causing blurring that would defeat the purpose of the high-resolution sensor, i.e. the laws of physics
impose a practical floor on how small the mask's features can be, thereby limiting the maximum achievable resolution before
diffraction renders the optical computation useless. Please comment.
Grayscale Information: The system's handling of grayscale (and color) is limited by two different components: the optical
mask and the sensor design, i.e. what the sensor can detect and what the mask can compute. The sensor's output is
quantized to 10-bit unsigned integers, allowing it to represent a range of intensity levels, not just black and white. In my
understanding, the significant bottleneck is that the optical mask is binary. Therefore, the convolution performed in the
optical domain is not a true multiplication-and-accumulation of numerical values. The system cannot perform optical
convolutions with grayscale kernels (e.g., a Sobel filter) and effectively binarizes the optical information before it reaches the
sensor. To handle complex grayscale data optically, the mask would need to be replaced by a more complex component
(kind of spatial light modulator), which could apply non-binary (grayscale) convolutional kernels. However, this would add
significant complexity, and cost, defeating the primary advantage of the NEOSTI approach.
Power Consumption: It is not fully clear to me what is included in the power consumption numbers of Table 1 and how
power consumption scales with e.g. increasing resolution. Some discussion on this point would be helpful as power
consumption seems to be a major KPI of this approach.
The paper does hint at future possibilities for overcoming these limitations, suggesting that scalability could be improved by:
Integrating lenses coated with specific patterns instead of a simple mask.
Expanding the number of optical layers by incorporating multiple, varied optical elements.
Leveraging advancements in material science, such as quantum dots, to create all-optical nonlinear responses, which could
allow for more complex computations beyond simple binary filtering.
In my view, a more in-depth discussion on how those extensions could address above limitations would improve the paper
significantly.

1.2 Reviewer 1 states:
The manuscript introduces the use of pulse width modulated (PWM) to encode light
intensity, which is then processed by on-chip units for arithmetic operations and
subsequent processing by a binary neural network (BNN) in a pipelined fashion without
the requirement of ADC. The computing process is all realized in digital domain. While
this is an interesting approach, since current in-memory computing strategies usually
conduct the matrix multiplication operation in analog domain by converting the signal
into an output voltage intensity, which is applicable to ANN with multi-valued weight

Our response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment.
Analog-domain computation methods typically rely on charge accumulation in
capacitors. Although such approaches allow for multi-bit weight configuration, the
calculation results are inevitably affected by analog noise, device mismatch, and
capacitor nonlinearity in the computing circuits, limiting the accuracy and reliability.
And the large capacitor arrays for analog-domain processing poses a conflict with the
area and power constraints of edge devices. In contrast, digital-domain computation is
inherently more robust, as it eliminates the influence of cumulative analog errors and
thus improve computational accuracy. Moreover, digital-domain computation allows
for more flexible architectural design and can readilytake advantage of the performance,
efficiency, and scalability gains brought by process technology improvements.
In our proposed PE, pulses generated by adjacent PWM pixels can be processed through
4
simple logic operations to control the readout counters, directly yielding results adapted
to BNN convolution, which reduces the power consumption of both pixel readout and
computation circuits. The PE design in this work is optimized specifically for BNN
models. Nevertheless, the concept of performing computation during the PWM pixel
readout process holds potential for further exploration and development, and it may be
extended to support a broader range of models and applications, such as edge detection
and image filtering, which similarly rely on spatially local pixel processing.

to be processed directly in the digital domain. Compared with analog-domain
computation based on capacitor-array integration, digital-domain computation is
inherently more robust, as it eliminates the influence of cumulative analog errors caused
by noise, device mismatch, and capacitor nonlinearity, ensuring the accuracy and
reliability of the processing results. Moreover, digital-domain computation allows for
more flexible architectural design. In NEOSTI, the Processing Element is elegantly
designed to couple the PWM readout process with the BNN computing framework,
achieving efficient in-pixel computation. The concept of integrating on-chip

1.3 Reviewer 1 states:
The system relies on a combination of in-sensor processing (PIS) and near-sensor
binary neural network (PNS) to handle dynamic scenes. The speed advantage of BNNs
in conducting dynamic tasks is not sufficiently discussed or demonstrated. A more
detailed analysis of these points would significantly strengthen the paper and improve
its clarity, such as the advantages of NEOSTI compares to established dynamic
processing approaches such as in-sensor or in-memory recurrent Neural Networks
(RNNs) or dynamic vision sensors (DVS). Also, is the time resolution of this NEOSTI
will be limited by the row-by-row exposure mode?
Our response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment.
The BNN model integrated in NEOSTI provides general, real-time, and efficient feature
extraction and compression capabilities, directly extracting compressed temporal
feature map sequences from input frames. The input image from the sensor has a
5
resolution of 64×64 with 10-bit precision in calculation mode, resulting in a data size
of 40,960 bits, while the output of on-chip BNN consists of 8 groups of 8×8 feature
maps quantized to 15 bits, with a total size of only 7,680 bits. As a result, BNN-based
feature extraction effectively compresses 81.3% of the input data scale, significantly
reducing the computational and storage overhead of frame feature sequences while
preserving intra-frame spatial features, which achieves a balance between spatial and
temporal feature processing abilities. In contrast, RNNs are good at sequence
processing but not well-suited for handling two-dimensional image data which has
strong local spatial correlations; DVS performs well in capturing rapidly changing or
moving scenes, but the event-stream output loses the global spatial features of each
frame. Both of them focus much on temporal feature analysis, lacking sufficient
capability to capture spatial features within frames. We have added the discussion of
dynamic processing in the revised manuscript.
The temporal resolution of NEOSTI is not constrained by the row-by-row exposure
mode, since the subsequent PIS and PNS convolution operations also require a row-by-
row sliding kernel for calculation. The global exposure mode would not improve
processing speed; instead, it would increase the overhead of readout and storage. In
NEOSTI, the exposure and subsequent BNN calculations are executed in a low-
overhead pipeline structure, ensuring that the acquired image can be processed row-by-
row in real time.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Image sensors in machine vision systems face significant challenges related to energy efficiency and processing capability when storing, transferring, and processing massive amounts of data. In humans, over 80% of brain-processed information is obtained through the eyes, which are capable of detecting and synchronously processing information with extremely low overall power consumption. Inspired by the biomimetics, we propose a Neuromorphic Electronic-Opto Spatial Temporal Imager (NEOSTI), one of the smallest electronic-opto fully integrated, eye-sized vision systems enabling acquisition and operation in typical indoor/outdoor non-coherent environments, under both natural and artificial lighting conditions without any extra requirement of the light source. NEOSTI combines processing-pre-sensor in optical domain, processing-in-sensor with nonlinear acquisition capability while optical to electronic converting, and processing-near-sensor in electronic domain, enabling parallel data computing capabilities while sensing. NEOSTI also integrates a low complexity Binary Neural Network to process image semantic information. It attains competitive performance in several visual processing tasks.

---

## Introduction

The human visual system is highly efficient in collecting and processing of the visible information. As a bionic device, the image sensor establishes a bridge between the real world in optical domain and artificial intelligence in electronic domain, but current image sensor technology falls short in meeting the requirement of real-time, low-power processing capability at the edge, which is critical for embodied intelligence such as intelligent robots, fully autonomous driving, and drones that require effective interaction with dynamic environments. Different processing technologies in either electronic domain or optical domain have been proposed in literature to break the bottleneck, but there is always a trade-off between processing performance and power/volume consumption.

Traditional artificial vision system relies on image sensors coupled with cloud processing or Artificial Intelligence (AI) processors, featuring higher image resolution, higher frame rate, and higher accuracy across various image processing tasks than human visual system, but paying for a several orders higher power consumption than the human visual system. In addition, the sub second wireless communication latency [1] between the sensor end and the computational cloud cannot meet the milliseconds to sub-milliseconds response time requirement risen from the embodied intelligence scenario.

In order to improve efficiency of the traditional artificial vision system, Processing-in-Sensor (PIS) [2–9] and Processing-Near-Sensor (PNS) [10–12] technologies have been introduced into the raw intensity acquisition process. PIS/PNS technology mitigates the delay and power consumption associated with redundant data transmission workload by integrating the sensing and computing components, enhances data processing efficiency as well as reduces the volume of data transmitted to the host through parallel processing at column or pixel levels. This approach aligns more closely with the operational principles of the visual systems observed in humans and various creatures. Nevertheless, the interdependence of the sensing and computing ends, influenced by the manufacturing process, implies that the performance of one end can impact the other, and the computing capabilities achievable on the sensing end are inherently limited.

In addition to PIS/PNS in electronic domain, optical domain calculation also provides a promising solution to increase computing speed without greatly increase the power consumption, as well as to overcome the bandwidth bottlenecks of PIS/PNS. In particular, the optical solution enables compression in the spatial domain of the image, resulting in a reduction of the amount of data to be processed on the sensor side. The development of the neural networks using optical methods, commonly referred to as optical neural networks (ONNs), has gained considerable traction as a prominent research area. Different ONNs have been proposed in literature [13–15], realizing parallel information processing by integrating optical architecture based on free space, aiming to accelerate deep learning computation. However, ONNs faces constraints related to power consumption, data rate, and on-chip processing capabilities. Additionally, many ONNs have restriction on light source, such as specific coherent light source, which cannot work in natural light condition.

In this article, we propose an all-in-one neuromorphic electronic-opto spatial-temporal image sensor (NEOSTI) design, which integrates various technologies to enhance data processing efficiency as well as to reduce sensor volume size. The NEOSTI integrated processing-pre-sensor(PPS) in optical domain, PIS with nonlinear acquisition capability and parallel data computing capabilities while sensing, and PNS with an on-chip binary neural network (BNN) for image semantic information processing. The NEOSTI attains competitive performance in five static and dynamic visual processing tasks. The experimental results reveal an accuracy of 96.4% in MNIST (10-category), 94.9% in UnityEyes (4-category), 91.7% in QuickDraw (10-category), 91.3% in Fashion MNIST (10-category), and 90.6% in Weizmann (video, 10-category), which demonstrate significant advancements in accuracy across multiple categories. These findings demonstrate a compact and efficient vision system with potential applications across a range of scenarios. Table 1 summarizes and compares the NEOSTI with representative frontier work in the fields discussed above. The NEOSTI is one of the smallest electronic-opto fully integrated vision systems that can operate in typical indoor and outdoor environments, under both natural and artificial lighting conditions, without any extra requirement of the light source, such as laser or coherent light source.

---

## Results

Architecture of NEOSTI

The human visual system (Fig.1a) enables efficient information compression while acquisition. There are over 130 million photoreceptor cells located in retina converting illumination intensity into neural spike signal. However, since a significant amount of pre-processing occurs within the retina itself [27], only about 1.2 million fibers (axons) are required in the optic nerve, resulting in an equivalent compression ratio of over 100. In addition, the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN) in the visual pathway plays a role in attenuating temporal correlations within the image, which further reduces the total amount of neural signals to be processed in the visual cortex. Secondly, the retina consumes only about 3 mW for both intensity acquisition and fundamental feature extraction [28], realizing a 23.08 pW/pixel energy efficiency. While state-of-the-art consumer image sensors only achieve an efficiency around 30 nW/pixel [29] for only intensity acquisition. In addition, the human visual system enables an intra-scene dynamic range (DR) of over 120 dB [28] and an inter-scene DR over 180 dB. While consumer image sensors typically achieve a DR of only 60-70 dB, the most advanced of which reaches around 140 dB [30].

Inspired by biomimetics, NEOSTI (Fig.1b) incorporates similar functionalities, including computations throughout the entire process, closely mimicking the capabilities of biological systems. The workflow of NEOSTI (Fig.1c) starts from a sliding convolution in the optical domain. A mask is deployed in front of the photodetector array in the electrical domain, filtering the input images and extracting the spatial features, which effectively reduces the amount of data received on the sensor plane. Subsequently, visual information is further processed using nonlinear optoelectronic conversion together with a calculation-supported readout link of the pixel circuit. At last, a low-complexity on-chip BNN is implemented as the visual cortex, providing high-level information processing capabilities, and finally obtaining the end-to-end classification result.

NEOSTI can be equivalent to an algorithm model (Fig.1d), which combines the optical domain and the electrical domain to construct a 3-layer sliding convolutional neural network. Initially, the 3-layer neural network model is trained to obtain the parameters for each part of the network. Subsequently, the parameters of the first layer’s 5 × 5 convolution kernel are extracted, binarized and solidified into physical patterns. The remaining of the network is reprogramed into a reconfigurable chip. The convolution mask and chip are co-packaged forming a lensless vision chip, which is capable of being fabricated using a mature process, making it well-suited for large-scale production.

Pre-sensor Processing in Optical Domain

The human eye (Fig.2a) perceives a world full of vibrant colors, while each animal has its distinct method of processing visual information. For instance, the compound eyes (Fig.2b) of flies are highly specialized, capable of capturing images at remarkable speeds. Their visual nervous system is adapted to rapidly process moving objects, enabling them to detect and react to their environment with high efficiency. Pre-processing occurs directly within the fly’s eyes for promptly responding to movement in their surroundings. Similarly, in frogs, specialized neurons in the retina are responsible for detecting edges or sudden motions within a scene. These neurons aid frogs in their survival strategies for hunting prey or evading predators. By filtering and integrating varying levels of light intensity and boundary information, a sophisticated feature detection is performed to ensure rapid and precise visual processing.

NEOSTI (Fig.2c) serves as the ”eyes” for machines, such as robots, facilitating intelligent processing across a variety of scenarios. It combines the capability of human eyes for the acquisition of the imaging of a scene, and compound eyes for feature extraction. The incident scene passes through four convolution kernels on the mask (Fig.2d), resulting in four feature maps on the sensor. The sliding convolution calculation is completed through the projection relationship of the geometric optics. Each pixel value on the feature map is obtained in parallel with near-zero latency. The schematic diagram of the equivalent optical calculation of the mask can be represented in a 5 × 5 binary matrix (Fig.2e). Assume that the input light source consists of a series of point light sources, by adjusting the distance from the mask to the imaging plane, each pixel on the imaging plane can receive the convolutional result between the point light source within a specific region and the convolution kernel parameters on the mask. As a result, the sensor plane receives four parallel convolution feature maps (Fig.2f). The feature size of the mask is limited by both diffraction and optical blur. (Fig.2g). Leveraging the propagation characteristics of geometric optics, this process can be effectively represented as a window sliding convolution, which is performed in parallel. The PPS operates at the position of the lens or glasses within the human visual system, augmenting the system’s capabilities and enabling direct processing of optical domain data, which is an attribute absence in the human visual system. By processing information in the optical domain, data arriving at the PIS module can be compressed with near-zero latency and zero power consumption, thereby reducing power consumption in both photoelectric conversion and data processing stages.

Neuromorphic Nonlinear Photoelectric Response

The retina, situated at the back of the eye, is a layered structure responsible for capturing light and initiating the process of vision (Fig.3a). The cones and rods in the lowest layer serve as photoreceptors, generating bio-signals associated with light intensity. The signal is then conveyed and transmitted through cells in the middle region of the retina. Ultimately, the generated nerve impulses are traveling along the optic nerve tract. The impulses are subsequently relayed to the visual cortex in the brain.

In a Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor, a reverse-biased photodiode structure is employed as the photoreceptors for photoelectric conversion (Fig.3d). The photodiode generates a photocurrent that is positively correlated with light intensity. A pre-reset capacitor is discharged by the photocurrent, causing the voltage VPD to decrease at a rate contingent upon the light intensity, realizing a conversion from optical intensity to electrical signals. The signals are subsequently amplified and read out by the associated circuit. Typically, a voltage-readout pixel structure is utilized. It is also known as the accumulation-mode pixel structure (Fig.3b), in which the voltage drop, ∆VPD, over a certain exposure time is measured and read out via an analog-to-digital convertor (ADC) to obtain the corresponding digital code value (Fig.3c), resulting in a linear relationship for the light-to-voltage conversion (gray line in Fig.3i).

Conversely, the human visual system employs a nonlinear relationship between the light intensity and perception is employed due to the nonlinearity of photoreceptor response (Fig.3j). This nonlinear characteristic effectively expands the visual capacity to a wider range of light levels, particularly in extremely bright or dim environments.

Inspired by the human vision system, NEOSTI utilizes a pulse width modulated (PWM) based 3-layered readout pixel structure [31–33] (Fig.3e), realizing a retina-mimicking nonlinear photoresponse and pulse-based representation of light intensity. The fundamental principle of the pulse modulation method starts with setting a voltage threshold at the configuration stage. A pulse flip was triggered when the voltage on the photodiode reaches the preset threshold VINV during the exposure process (Fig.3f). This approach enables a nonlinear light-to-time conversion without the requirement of ADC, and allows operation at lower voltages. The pulse output format also facilitates low-power computation design at the circuit level processing, which will be discussed in the following section. To further align the nonlinear response of PWM pixel with the human eye, a dynamic scanning bias voltage, VG, is applied at point G (Fig.3g), making the threshold of the flipping voltage VINV to gradually increase over time. Compared to a fixed flipping voltage threshold, dynamic VINV stretches the response curve in low-light intensity ranges, extending the dynamic range of pixel under dark light condition (Fig.3h-i). Experimental results indicate that the PWM pixels of NEOSTI exhibit a nonlinear photoresponse function similar to that of visual cells to encode light intensity information (Fig.3k). Moreover, the simulated responses demonstrate that by adjusting the bias voltage VG, the pixel has the potential to mimic the adaptive function of the human eye, shifting the curve as a whole to accommodate varying lighting conditions (Fig.3l).

In-Sensor and Near-Sensor Processing

Behind the photosensitive area, an array of processing elements (PEs) is employed to receive the pulse signal, enabling parallel visual information in-sensor processing. The processing element is simultaneously connected to two adjacent PWM pixels (Fig.4a), performing direct summation or subtraction calculation on the two pulse signals from two neighboring pixels based on programmable parameters during the exposure process. The working times of the two counters within the PE are non-overlapping (Fig.4b), which reduces the counters’ working duration by 33% compared to conventional readout methods, lowering circuit dynamic power consumption. The summation calculation is performed using a left-shift module for efficient ”×2” operation, and a digital adder to sum the digital codes, while the subtraction calculation relies solely on counter DIFF, allowing counter SUM to be disabled to achieve greater performance advantages. The overall in-sensor processing forms part of a 2 × 2 binary convolution with a stride of 1, which effectively removes spatial-temporal redundancy and extract fundamental features from the input data.

Additionally, a BNN is implemented on-chip, providing advanced near-sensor information processing capabilities, and enhancing the ability to generalize across various tasks. Due to the concurrent exposure of each row of pixels and the simultaneous generation of intra-row calculation results by parallel PEs, the implementation of a pipeline architecture becomes imperative to efficiently execute convolution operations. A 4-stage pipeline dedicated to a convolution block (Fig.4c) is utilized in NEOSTI. The block encompasses a 2 × 2 convolution layer, a ReLU nonlinear activation function, and a 2 × 2 maximum pooling layer. This pipelined architecture is compactly parallelized, fully utilizing the row-by-row exposure time of the pixels to complete the pipeline operations without any additional time overhead, maximizing the utilization of on-chip hardware resources with high computational efficiency. There are in total two layers of convolution and pooling operations performed through the in-sensor and the near-sensor processing, yielding the fully-processed feature maps. By leveraging on-chip storage capabilities, the difference between frames can be directly calculated, which is a commonly-used operation for inter-frame processing. Combined with subsquent pipelined BNN structure, NEOSTI is endowed with enhanced ability for processing spatial-temporal hybrid information.

Evaluation of NEOSTI system

The performance of NEOSTI has been validated across multiple tasks, including MNIST[34], Fashion MNIST[35], Quick Draw[36] and UnityEyes[37], with an accuracy of 96.4%, 91.3%, 91.7%, and 94.9%, respectively (Fig.5a). In experiments, the opticalmaskkeptthesameconvolutionpattern,whiletheparametersofelectricallayerswere reconfigured for different tasks. The experimental results not only show the recognition performance of NEOSTI on various tasks, but also demonstrate that the programmableelectricalconvolutionlayersprovideNEOSTIwithgoodgeneralization ability between different tasks.

In order to further verify the respective functions of each part of NEOSTI, differentsetups,includingexperimentsusingonlyPPSoronlyPIS,wereverifiedseparately (Fig.5b). The NEOSTI shows an average accuracy improvement of 11.725% and 14.075%comparedwithonlyPISoronlyPPS.ComparedwithLeNet-5,asmallneural network in the digital domain, NEOSTI shows similar performance. In addition, we also verified the noise robustness of NEOSTNI (Fig.5c) using the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) calculated as
PSNR=10·log(MAXI)2/MSE=20·log(MAXI/√MSE) (1)
where MAXI represents the maximum pixel value, and MSE represents the noise level. When the light intensity becomes lower, the PSNR deteriorates. Experimental results show that when the PSNR decreases, NEOSTI does not significantly deteriorate in the accuracy of different characters. This feature is advantageous due to the fact that the optical domain processing enables the filtration of a portion of the noise. Furthermore, the neural network’s robust anti-interference capability enables better performance, particularly in low-light photo scenarios.

In addition to static image classification task, NEOSTI was also tested on the video analysis task, which requires not only the capability of spatial information acquistion, but also the capability of temporal information analysis between frames. NEOSTI is evaluated on an open dataset, Weizmann [38]. The Weizmann dataset (Fig.5d) includes multiple video sequences of ten different actions, including run, jump, bend, etc. In each video sequence, only one person performs the action. NEOSTI can convert sequence information into several feature maps (Fig.5g), with an accuracy of 90.6% (Fig.5e). The BNN-based feature extraction model serves as a general, real-time, and efficient data compressor that effectively reduces the input data volume by 81.3%, significantly reducing the computational and storage overhead of feature sequences while preserving intra-frame spatial features. In different-setup experiments, the only PPS setup shows a 58% accuracy on the same dataset (Fig.5f). This is mainly due to the fact that the processing of the optical domain is spatially without storage. The programmable on-chip PIS and PNS circuits can make up for this. Similarly to the test on static image classification task, when noise increases, NEOSTI exhibits good robustness (Fig.5h). The spatial domain filtering of the PPS module still plays a key role in processing noise.

### Reviewer 3

The approach presented in this paper is certainly interesting from a scientific perspective. Splitting operations and layers of a
CNN-type network for image data processing (image recognition/classification tasks) between different physical elements
like static optical masks, focal-plane/pixel-level analog signal processing and binary neural network layers operated in the
digital domain, is an interesting and novel concept worth to be published. The presentation of innovation is sufficiently well
done, the idea, concept and methodology are well described and illustrated. Evaluation results are presented. However,
several points need to be addressed, in particular the discussion section is very weak and misses out on several key
questions.
In my view, at least these points below need to be addressed before possible publication of this material:
(1) Some claims are bold or imprecise:
"the smallest all-in-one eye size fully integrated vision system", The presented vision system, with chip dimensions of 5mm x
5mm is certainly not "the smallest" ever proposed. Just as one of many examples, Synsens's Speck vision System-on-Chip
combines a 128x128 (event-based) pixel array with a 9-layer spiking CNN processor on 30mm2 silicon.
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06793)
"Near-human performance in five static and dynamic visual processing tasks" — "near human" is a very bold statement,
particularly given the toy-problem like nature of the experiments/data sets used for validation of the NEOSTI approach, see
below (4).
"current image sensor technology falls short in meeting the requirement of embodied intelligence", a broad statement without
any clear meaning. Later, "embodied intelligence" is vaguely defined as possibly involving e.g. "intelligent robots, fully
autonomous driving, drones..."
"NEOSTI utilizes a pulse width modulated (PWM) based non-linear readout pixel structure, realizing a retina-like 3-layered
processing structure to generate pulse signals analogous to neural spikes" — NEOSTI is far from being "retina-like" or from
generating anything resembling "neural spikes". This is per se not a problem but does not need to be claimed this way.
(2) More issues not related to technical content that need attention:
Several language-related flaws: E.g. "NEOSTI is ... system that can operable ...", "lenless" — proof reading required
Factually imprecise statements: "consumer image sensor can only achieve a DR around 140dB" — no, consumer imagers
typically reach 60-70dB, only specialized automotive multi-exposure image sensors go up to DR levels around/beyond
140dB"
Citations and benchmarking: NEOSTI claims to be "neuromorphic" but does not compare itself to any other neuromorphic
vision solutions (e.g. event sensor based) that can solve similar problems; e.g. Synsense's Speck, combining event pixel
array and SNN processor on a single chip (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06793) nor with SoA industry Vision System-on-chip
solutions like Sony's IMX500, targeting similar use cases/applications (https://www.aitrios.sony-semicon.com/edge-ai-
devices/imx500).
Pulse modulation (including PWM) is a well known approach in vision sensing — prior work should be cited (e.g.
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5701724).
(3) Missing discussion on Static mask limitations:
Looking at the early feature extraction capabilities of NEOSTI, the static optical mask functions as the first convolutional
layer of a 3-layer convolutional neural network. The features it extracts are likely some fundamentally low-level spatial
features, determined by the patterns etched onto the mask itself. The mask performs a 5x5 sliding convolution on the
incoming light. I assume that this process is analogous to the initial feature extraction step in a typical CNN, which often
identifies basic elements like edges, corners, and textures. In the present case, the weights, implemented as the patterns on
the mask, are binary (transparent or opaque) and are derived from the pre-trained weights of a Binary Neural Network
(BNN). This means the mask is optimized for the types of features relevant to its original training data. For a different use
case requiring the detection of fundamentally different low-level features, a new mask would need to be fabricated. So, while
this optical pre-processing is highly efficient in terms of power and speed, a static, fabricated mask does present limitations
regarding flexibility and the range of addressable use cases.
In my view, a deeper discussion on this subject is missing and should include:
Lack of Adaptability: The mask itself cannot adapt to changing conditions or tasks at run-time. The system's adaptability
relies on the programmable on-chip electronic circuits (PIS and PNS) that process the feature maps created by the static
mask.
Potential for Sub-Optimal Performance on Unseen Tasks: The fixed front-end filtering might be sub-optimal for tasks that
were not considered during the initial training and mask design. The success of the system on a new task depends on
whether the features extracted by the fixed mask are still relevant and sufficiently informative for the subsequent electronic
layers to work with.
The paper suggests some kind of modular approach where optical components could be interchanged via a standardized
interface, allowing for task versatility. This implies that for different applications, one could swap out the mask for another
one with more suitable pre-trained patterns. How could such an approach be implemented in a real-world / commercial
scenario? I believe some in-depth discussion on these points would significantly increase the quality and impact of the
paper.
(4) Insufficient discussion on Adaptability and Scalability:
In my understanding, the presented implementation as described seems to have a limited real-world applicability. The
concept (in the form of a fabricated prototype) is validated only on "toy problems", using very low-resolution input data with
only simple high-contrast grey scale or BW features. (MNIST, UnityEyes, QuickDraw, Fashion MNIST, Weizmann), and the
NEOSTI approach, in its current form, would face considerable challenges when applied to more complex, higher-resolution,
and full grayscale natural scenes. The limitations I think is the binary optical mask.
Higher-Resolution Features: Scaling to a higher resolution would present a physical challenge due to light diffraction. The
minimum feature size that can be created on the optical mask is governed by the wavelength of light and the distance
between the mask and the sensor. Currently, the feature size is set to 40µm. To increase the image resolution, the pixels on
the sensor would need to be made smaller and more numerous. Consequently, the features on the mask would also need to
shrink to match this new, finer pixel grid. However, as the feature size shrinks, the diffraction of light becomes a more
significant issue, causing blurring that would defeat the purpose of the high-resolution sensor, i.e. the laws of physics
impose a practical floor on how small the mask's features can be, thereby limiting the maximum achievable resolution before
diffraction renders the optical computation useless. Please comment.
Grayscale Information: The system's handling of grayscale (and color) is limited by two different components: the optical
mask and the sensor design, i.e. what the sensor can detect and what the mask can compute. The sensor's output is
quantized to 10-bit unsigned integers, allowing it to represent a range of intensity levels, not just black and white. In my
understanding, the significant bottleneck is that the optical mask is binary. Therefore, the convolution performed in the
optical domain is not a true multiplication-and-accumulation of numerical values. The system cannot perform optical
convolutions with grayscale kernels (e.g., a Sobel filter) and effectively binarizes the optical information before it reaches the
sensor. To handle complex grayscale data optically, the mask would need to be replaced by a more complex component
(kind of spatial light modulator), which could apply non-binary (grayscale) convolutional kernels. However, this would add
significant complexity, and cost, defeating the primary advantage of the NEOSTI approach.
Power Consumption: It is not fully clear to me what is included in the power consumption numbers of Table 1 and how
power consumption scales with e.g. increasing resolution. Some discussion on this point would be helpful as power
consumption seems to be a major KPI of this approach.
The paper does hint at future possibilities for overcoming these limitations, suggesting that scalability could be improved by:
Integrating lenses coated with specific patterns instead of a simple mask.
Expanding the number of optical layers by incorporating multiple, varied optical elements.
Leveraging advancements in material science, such as quantum dots, to create all-optical nonlinear responses, which could
allow for more complex computations beyond simple binary filtering.
In my view, a more in-depth discussion on how those extensions could address above limitations would improve the paper
significantly.
